content:
In light of the recent soundness issues found in the Lean kernel, @Joachim Breitner and I have made a plan of desired changes to the kernel that should make it more robust. This list can be found in this meta issue. Such changes include making the level equality algorithm complete, adapting Lean's type theory and implementation to have decidable equality, and making sort-polymorphic inductive types behave better with regards to large elimination and projections. Any feedback on these changes is very welcomed :slight_smile:

(Pinging people that might be interested in interacting with this: @Mario Carneiro @Talia Ringer @Meven Lennon-Bertrand @Jean Abou Samra @Jason Rute @Chris Bailey )
To structure the discussion a bit: #Type theory > Kernel renovation: Level normalization

Thanks for writing this up @Arthur Adjedj ! Very happy to see suggestions to improve Lean informed by theory.

One question: I'm very ignorant of all of the intricacies of Lean, but it was my impression that it was essentially impossible to have a Lean-like (definitional proof irrelevance, impredicative Prop, etc) type theory with good metatheoretic properties unless one goes the observational type theory route. Was my impression wrong or is there a key new idea in your suggestions that overcomes this?

The story around having decidable equality for Lean's type theory is a bit convoluted, but the gist of it is that

  1. Restricting recursive predicates like Acc to not be large-eliminating and
  2. Ensuring Eq.rec reduces "the right way" (i.e without ever needing to reduce an equality proof)

Are enough to have a type theory whose judgemental equality is decidable, these two insights are discussed in these two papers respectively: Definitional Proof Irrelevance Made Accessible and Consolidating Equality in a Proof Irrelevant Universe
(meta-note: I think we should relocate discussion of the metatheory of lean4 kernel to #lean4lean , including the parts that involve coordination with lean4 FRO or changes to the lean4 kernel)
I cannot move topics, and don't care otherwise. If you feel strongly about this, just move them as desired.
This topic was moved here from #Type theory > Lean Kernel Renovation by Mario Carneiro.

Naive Questions since you mention “soundness”:

  1. to what extent do these changes improve soundness (both theoretical soundness and actual elimination of bugs in the kernel)?
  2. One of @Talia Ringer ‘s complaints is that Lean’s inductive is not specified and of course you can’t prove (formally or informally) that inductives are sound, nor can you write a kernel matching a spec which doesn’t exist. So:
    1. Does this fully specify the inductive types?
    2. If so, Can one write this spec explicitly in lean4lean?
    3. Can one prove the full type theory spec is consistent with the set theoretic model approach? Can one (building off of @Kim Morrison ‘s prior work) vibe proof that fully consistency result in lean4lean-model?
    4. Does this happen to match lean-inductive-model in that each inductive type is (in some sense I’m having trouble making precise) equivalent to the lean-inductive-model interpretation? (I’m just curious. It doesn’t matter in the end.)
  3. Is it easy to make these changes in lean4lean and prove it correct?
  4. What soundness work remains to be done?

(1) I think the obvious answer to the soundness question is that we will have eliminated the vast majority of possible future theoretical soundness bugs and a significant majority of implementation soundness bugs if we finish the proof of lean4lean. The suggested changes will make that proof easier (and some of them are already assumed by lean4lean)

1. I would say most of these changes improve completeness of the system rather than soundness. In practice, soundness issues related to the lack of transitivity in Lean's definitional equality have been found recently (e.g lean4#14807), so making the system behave better relative to its theory ensures less weird things in such corners can happen
  2. This doesn't specify inductive types, though a spec can definitely be written in Lean4Lean, and I want to commit some time in helping do so in the near future. I also believe the spec around projections and eta might be made easier with these changes, as projections can be always be written using recursors with these changes (@Mario Carneiro might have a relevant opinion on this). I don't have an answer to 2.3 and 2.4
  3. These changes should not make things in Lean4Lean much harder to manage, or at least I would like to believe so ? again, @Mario Carneiro is better suited to answer this, and the current plan can be tweaked to accommodate Lean4Lean better if need be.
  4. If you mean from the theory side, I would say everything missing in Lean4Lean. If you mean from an implementation POV, the way nested types are handled is not planned to change in the near future, and is definitely the weirdest part of the kernel IMO, although many additional checks have been added to that pass recently to ensure it produces well-typed types/constructors/recursors. A potential future change would be to get rid of the mutual<->nested translation which is currently implemented to something more robust, but that would be a big breaking change and would require a lot of adaptation from all kernels, including Lean4Lean, as well as the elaborator.
On (3) I think most changes under consideration don't make a big difference one way or another. Anything that makes type checking decidable will have a significant impact on the metatheory though
Thanks! (And I should have noticed nest types were not mentioned.)

I'm not sure how we should handle the rollout of changes that impact the input format (e.g. additional flags in inductive specs, or changes to the recursor shape for existing legal inputs). I'm inclined to suggest that we should front-load those changes - it's difficult for lean4lean to express those changes itself since it uses the same input type as the lean kernel itself

Anything that makes type checking decidable will have a significant impact on the metatheory though

A positive one I would hope ? The scope for the metatheory work does not have to change because of type-checking becoming decidable, though it would open the door for proving more things such as negative soundness of the implementation, if the property was to now hold true
that will also presumably impact the growing ecosystem of external kernels if it changes the lean4export format

Arthur Adjedj said:

Anything that makes type checking decidable will have a significant impact on the metatheory though

A positive one I would hope ? The scope for the metatheory work does not have to change because of type-checking becoming decidable, though it would open the door for proving more things such as negative soundness of the implementation, if the property was to now hold true

not necessarily, since it strengthens the target theorem we want to prove
so it may be more work
on the other hand, I think the metatheory is more well understood so we might make it to the end faster

Mario Carneiro said:

I'm not sure how we should handle the rollout of changes that impact the input format (e.g. additional flags in inductive specs, or changes to the recursor shape for existing legal inputs). I'm inclined to suggest that we should front-load those changes - it's difficult for lean4lean to express those changes itself since it uses the same input type as the lean kernel itself

I think the general plan is to prepare PRs for each part of the meta issue, and set a certain Lean release for which all of these would be merged. The rollout work could be done in sync with external kernels and Lean4Export, ensuring everything is ready on all fronts before merging.
well by front-load I mean we should consider making format changes before the metatheory work that motivates them

Mario Carneiro schrieb:

that will also presumably impact the growing ecosystem of external kernels if it changes the lean4export format

Yes, hence the last paragraph on the issue: I hope we can bundle all these changes in one Lean release, so that external checkers can do all the changes in one go. The export format will change, too.
because it is easier for lean4lean to be able to work on the metatheory after the format change has already landed
and the theory change should probably happen only once the lean4lean metatheory work is done or near-done

Mario Carneiro said:

not necessarily, since it strengthens the target theorem we want to prove

Would it need to be strengthened or is it simply that it could be done so once the theory becomes better behaved ?

Mario Carneiro schrieb:

and the theory change should probably happen only once the lean4lean metatheory work is done or near-done

Here I disagree. I don’t want more on the critical path to landing these than necessary for these fixes, and would not want to block on either theory or external checkers. Implementation wise there is hopefully enough head warning that checkers will be able to adjust (and hopefully the changes aren't that invasive to non-verified checkers like nanoda).

What's the exact target other than positive soundness of the implementation relative to the theory in practice ? If the theory was to become decidable, negative soundness could also be in reach, but I would argue this be an orthogonal goal altogether. @Meven Lennon-Bertrand any thoughts on this ?

The more the better, but the whole idea of what I've been going towards in the last years is to separate the kernel's verification in multiple chunks that give increasing specification of what it's doing. So agreed that negative soundness/partial correctness is good to have but orthogonal, and definitely less critical than positive soundness, which reduces "the kernel cannot prove False" to "the theory cannot prove False", and is the main target here I feel.
Positive soundness is all you need to deduce "the kernel cannot prove false" from "the theory cannot prove false"
For Quot, is it proposed to have Quot.{u} {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Sort (max 1 u)? Or Quot.{u} {α : Type u} (r : α → α → Prop) : Type u
I would say the former, for the sake of backwards compatibility, although I'm not sure quotients over propositions are used much in practice.
It would be interesting to see how much breaks when large elimination is disallowed for Acc.

I would expect not much, since well-founded functions already don't reduce, and they're the main use-case for Acc. Perhaps the generation of equational lemmas for well-founded functions becomes harder with this change ? @Joachim Breitner

Large elimination removal is already staged at lean4#13851 (elab changes) and the stacked lean4#14892 (kernel changes). The first can land any time between “nobody spoke up in time against the change” and when we actually change the kernel.

Not sure if someone has found this before but:

example (x : PUnit.{0}) : PUnit.rec.{2, 0} (motive := fun _ => Type) Nat x = Nat := rfl -- fail
example (x : True) : True.rec.{2} (motive := fun _ => Type) Nat x = Nat := rfl -- succeed

Because apparently the K-like check doesn't substitute levels before checking.
I discovered this in the process of looking at the incompleteness of the slow-checker of metalean
It does appear to be intended behaviour though, AFAICT "k-like" eligibility is a static property of an inductive declaration. This is just really ugly
